A secret sharing scheme is defined by its access structure, which specifies the qualified subsets of participants capable of recovering the secret. The universal access structure represents the most efficient configuration for a given set of participants and secrets, as it minimizes the information entropy held by any group of players. This structure is determined by the intersection graph of the unqualified subsets. This paper demonstrates that the optimal arrangement corresponds to a random access structure, where all unqualified subsets consist of exactly the same number of participants. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal configuration is achieved when these subsets are nearly uniform in size, meaning their cardinalities differ by at most one.

We present an approach for precisely measuring the entanglement of two-photon polarization qubits by performing joint projective measurements on multiple independent copies of the state. Utilizing a convex combination of two specific joint observables, this method reaches optimal precision for any entangled two-photon state when employing quantum cloning for the necessary copies. Our findings indicate that for all entangled two-photon states, the variance of a single appropriately chosen observable matches the quantum Cramér–Ramer lower bound, meaning optimal precision can be attained without cloning by simply measuring one universal observable.

In the context of the drift-reduced Hasegawa-Wakatani model, we investigate the dynamics of localized structures, specifically current ribs, which are responsible for transporting parallel currents. Utilizing a reduced toroidal aspect ratio model, we simulate turbulence in the edge region of tokamaks. Our analysis examines the formation, evolution, and dissipation of these current ribs, with a particular focus on their interaction with the nonlinear transport of heat and particles.

This paper introduces a novel, straightforward, and efficient method for continuing deep learning on images. The approach involves training a lightweight adapter network to classify new data while keeping a pretrained model's backbone frozen. We demonstrate that this technique effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and reduces the risk of negative transfer compared to existing methods. The simplicity of the framework allows it to be easily integrated into various existing continual learning paradigms. Experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 datasets confirm that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

Growing online hate speech has led to severe outcomes, including radicalization and hate crimes, prompting a need for automated detection systems. While existing approaches focus on detection, they often overlook the nuances of language within hate speech, specifically sarcasm. This study addresses that gap by introducing a novel dataset comprising 1,000 manually annotated instances of sarcastic hate speech in English. We further evaluate several state-of-the-art models for detection, demonstrating that incorporating contextual information significantly enhances performance. Our analysis reveals that contextual embeddings, such as those from BERT, outperform traditional models like LSTM and BiLSTM. Additionally, we assess various BERT variants, including BERT, BERT, and BERT, finding that BERT achieves the best results. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating contextual data to effectively identify sarcastic hate speech.

This study examines oscillatory behavior within large-scale inhibitory networks utilizing the mean-field approximation. We demonstrate that oscillations, which are typically absent in networks with Poisson-distributed connections, emerge when the degree distribution is sufficiently broadened. Specifically, we derive an analytical expression for the minimum frequency in these networks and identify a lower bound for the required distribution width. Additionally, we explore the impact of incorporating a refractory period, showing that it amplifies oscillatory amplitudes and increases the corresponding frequencies.

This paper introduces a novel program repair technique leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The approach utilizes a GAN to synthesize candidate fixes for bugs, with an adversarial network trained to identify non-viable repairs to guide the generator toward valid solutions. The proposed method was evaluated on the GitHub Repair Research Repository (GH-RRR) dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art repair systems.

This paper introduces a novel method for lower-bounding capacity in interference channels, grounded in a fresh definition of spectral inf-mutual information rates. These rates quantify the minimal achievable mutual information between two processes, regardless of the length of their causal history, when generated by any causal mutual information generator. We demonstrate that the resulting spectral inf-mutual information rate capacity region upper-bounds the actual channel capacity. Furthermore, we provide a straightforward algorithm to compute these limits for channels with finite-state channels, demonstrating through examples that this approach often surpasses traditional outer bounds.

The Equation-of-State (EOS) of nuclei is a fundamental property that dictates the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, such as those found in heavy-ion collisions. This study investigates the flow coefficients ($v_n$) in $^{124}\text{Te}+^{124}\text{Te}$ collisions at 33 A MeV/A, utilizing the ALADIN array. The observed $p_T$-dependent $v_2$ and $v_3$ align well with predictions from the relativistic quantum molecular dynamics (RQMD) model, which incorporates a soft EOS. Furthermore, the study examines the $p_T$-dependence of $v_n$ for various particle species, including protons, deuterons, and light fragments, to assess their sensitivity to the Equation-of-State.

Early identification of COVID-19 cases is crucial for curbing the virus's spread and reducing the burden on medical facilities. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to detect COVID-19 from chest X-ray images by integrating two specialized CNN architectures, DenseNet152 and EfficientNetB3, through feature fusion. The model's efficacy was validated using the ISIC-MED dataset, which comprises 1,408 chest X-ray scans categorized into three groups: COVID-19 positive, pneumonia, and normal. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 90.11% for classifying COVID-19 images and 89.89% for pneumonia images.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a promising solution for wireless communication tasks, offering the ability to learn from graph-structured data. However, their application in this domain faces significant hurdles, including the need for extensive labeled datasets, susceptibility to adversarial attacks, and a lack of interpretability. To overcome these barriers, this paper introduces a novel framework leveraging self-supervised learning to train GNNs for wireless systems using unlabeled data. The proposed method features a self-supervised learning module that generates training samples via a self-generated task, alongside a graph convolutional network designed to map these samples to a high-dimensional feature space. The framework's efficacy is validated through two key applications: channel estimation in massive MIMO systems and graph-based resource allocation for non-orthogonal multiple access. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised methods while simultaneously offering enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks.

Brazil ranks as the second nation globally for homicide rates, with Black men aged 15 to 29 comprising the most affected demographic. This study introduces a novel methodology to analyze homicide data by integrating spatial and temporal dimensions. The approach involves a two-stage process: initially, a clustering algorithm identifies high-risk zones, and subsequently, a classification model predicts the probability of homicide occurrence within those areas based on socio-economic indicators. The results indicate that homicide incidents are not randomly distributed but are instead concentrated in specific zones, which vary across different time periods.

This paper investigates the convergence behavior of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with adaptively adjusted, exponentially decaying step-sizes applied to smooth, strongly-convex functions, where the exact optimal step-size remains unknown. We demonstrate that this variant achieves an optimal mean-square convergence rate of $O(1/t)$ and an optimal mean-expectation convergence rate of $O(1/t)$, matching the performance guarantees of the standard SGD algorithm. Furthermore, we establish that the mean-expectation convergence rate for the adaptive step-size SGD is optimal in the sense of lower bounds.

Axion models serve as a primary solution to the strong-CP problem, yet they face challenges regarding their axion mass, which may be too large to align with the cosmic axion dark matter abundance. To resolve this, we introduce a framework based on non-Abelian gauge-portal dark matter, which naturally accommodates a lighter axion. Our model achieves two key objectives: it provides a viable mechanism for the misalignment dark matter scenario and ensures dark matter stability through a $Z_2$ symmetry. Additionally, the framework allows for extensive phenomenological exploration, including potential detection at the Large Hadron Collider and astrophysical signatures, such as axion-photon conversion in magnetized environments.

This study investigates the thermodynamics of a memory mechanism operating under non-equilibrium conditions, specifically focusing on a single particle confined within a time-varying potential. We analyze the work and heat exchanges associated with both the initialization and erasure of memory, as well as the information generation during the initialization phase. Our findings demonstrate that the total information generated during initialization is equal to the information destroyed during erasure. This result contrasts with the standard Landau limit by decoupling memory erasure from initialization, thereby permitting a more efficient process. We validate this mechanism through a proposed setup involving a particle suspended by a molecular spring, which is actuated by an external time-dependent force.

Grasping remains a fundamental yet difficult challenge in robotics, particularly when requiring dexterity. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often rely on limited, manually curated datasets that lack diversity in object shapes, textures, and lighting conditions. To address this, we introduce DexGraspNet, a large-scale dataset featuring over 1.5 million successful grasp attempts across 10,000 objects, capturing data from 12 cameras at 200 frames per second. This work also presents a novel deep learning architecture that utilizes this comprehensive data to predict both the success probability and the full 6-degree-of-freense pose for dexterous grasping. Our model is trained and evaluated against various real-world objects and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods.

This paper introduces a novel MRI imaging technique designed to mitigate respiratory motion, which is achieved by reconstructing data from a non-uniformly and sparsely sampled $k$-space. The method relies on two primary assumptions: first, that the image remains stationary during a single breath cycle; and second, that the image can be sparsely represented in a transform domain. To enforce these constraints, we developed a new iterative algorithm that iteratively refines the reconstruction by alternating between a transform step and a data consistency update. The transform step generates an initial estimate by segmenting the image into multiple sub-regions corresponding to different respiratory phases, each assumed to be static, and then combining them to form a continuous representation of the full breathing cycle. The data consistency update then fills missing $k$-space samples by calculating the Fourier transform of this synthesized breathing motion. To further enhance robustness, we incorporated a total variation (TV) penalty into the data fidelity step to suppress noise and artifacts. Experimental results using both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that this approach effectively recovers high-quality images from incomplete $k$-space data, successfully compensating for respiratory motion.

Knowledge distillation serves as a powerful strategy for compressing models by transferring knowledge from a large teacher network to a compact student architecture. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages the inherent structural similarities between teacher and student networks to facilitate more effective knowledge transfer. By aligning the weights of corresponding filters within convolutional layers, the proposed method enables the student to directly access the teacher's learned features. Empirical results demonstrate that this filter alignment technique yields superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art distillation methods.

This paper investigates the relationship between regular foliations and regular open sets, demonstrating that the topological equivalence of two regular foliations implies the topological equivalence of their corresponding regular open sets. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a homeomorphism that maps the open set of one function onto another while preserving the associated foliation structure.

Grassland degradation is a critical challenge in arid and semi-arid regions, driven by the complex interplay between vegetation patterns and grazing intensity. This study employs a reaction-diffusion model to explore how spatially distributed vegetation influences local grazing dynamics. The analysis reveals that vegetation patterns significantly affect the local intensity of grazing, a finding supported by numerical simulations. Furthermore, the study examines the stability of homogeneous vegetation states and assesses how variations in water supply and diffusion rates impact vegetation coverage.

CountSketch is a well-established randomized sketching technique that approximates the top-$k$ frequent items within a data stream using $O(k)$ space. This paper introduces a variant called **Adaptive CountSketch**, which dynamically adjusts its parameters based on the specific characteristics of the input stream. This adaptation allows the algorithm to achieve improved time and space complexities compared to the original method. We evaluate the performance of this new algorithm against the standard CountSketch across three distinct scenarios: (1) streams containing a fixed number of elements, (2) streams where the number of distinct elements is unknown, and (3) streams where the distribution of element frequencies is known. Our findings demonstrate that, in all three cases, the proposed method outperforms the original CountSketch in terms of efficiency.

We introduce a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) software suite designed to facilitate rapid prototyping and the development of novel algorithms. Built upon the fixed-node AFQMC framework, this program leverages the stochastic reconfiguration technique to ensure numerical stability. It supports various interaction models, including the Hubbard, multi-orbital Hubbard, and infinite-$U$ models, as well as the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model. Performance benchmarks on standard chemical systems demonstrate that our code achieves efficiency comparable to established C++ implementations, while offering superior capabilities for parallelization and the integration of advanced features.

This paper examines the link between high-frequency trading (HFT) and game theory, specifically focusing on Nash Equilibrium and Pareto-optimality. It demonstrates that HFT represents a pursuit of the Nash Equilibrium, arguing that achieving this state is essential for reaching Pareto-optimal outcomes. The authors contend that HFT acts as a mechanism facilitating the transition toward these game-theoretic ideals. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between the Nash Equilibrium and the Efficient Market Hypothesis, positing that the former aids in validating the latter. The work concludes by addressing the limitations of both the Nash Equilibrium and the Efficient Market Hypothesis, while also outlining potential future research avenues.

This paper addresses the optimal pricing problem for a seller dealing with $n$ buyers, where private valuations follow an i.i.d. distribution over $[0,1]$. We examine two scenarios: first, selling $m$ identical items drawn from arbitrary distributions, and second, selling $m$ distinct items where valuations adhere to a log-concave distribution. For identical items, we propose a randomized mechanism that achieves a constant approximation ratio of the social welfare, assuming valuations are drawn from identical distributions. When items differ, we present a mechanism that maintains a constant approximation ratio if all buyers share the same log-concave valuation distribution. Furthermore, we extend these results to settings where buyers' valuations are drawn from distinct distributions.

Abstractive summarization aims to generate summaries that are both concise and informative. Although current state-of-the-art models produce fluent text, they often fail to deliver specific details. To address this, we introduce a novel approach utilizing Entity Chains (ECs)—graph structures that represent semantic relationships among entities—to guide the generation process. By training the model to incorporate ECs directly, we enable it to ingest chain information and output summaries with higher entity specificity. Our experiments demonstrate that this method achieves significant improvements in specificity, particularly for summaries requiring detailed entity information.
This paper establishes weaker yet sufficient criteria for differentiating an n-variable real-valued function by building upon the properties of its (n-1)-variable counterpart.

Vocal entrainment serves as a critical indicator of human interaction, offering valuable insights into the cognitive and behavioral traits of speakers. This study introduces a novel method for automatically detecting vocal entrainment by modeling the dynamic interplay between speakers. The approach utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to capture short-term dependencies in speech signals, followed by a deep belief network (DBN) to extract high-level features from these outputs. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents an original proof of semantic consistency for the quantum lambda calculus ($\lambda_{QM}$), utilizing a method of realizability tailored for a quantum domain. This approach is a modified version of a technique previously introduced by Hyland and Plotkin in their work on PCF. By employing this method, we achieve two significant outcomes: first, we establish a continuous, semantic, and injective mapping from the syntax to the semantics of the language, and second, we demonstrate that the semantic continuity property holds. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the semantics of the quantum lambda calculus are equivalent to those of the untyped lambda calculus, which in turn are equivalent to the PCF semantics.

This work examines the low-energy excitations of systems with a small number of electrons at the $\nu=1/3$ filling factor, utilizing the framework established by composite fermions and composite bosons. We demonstrate that the composite fermion model accurately predicts the calculated quasiparticle energies, whereas the composite bosion model fails to do so. The study further confirms that the entropy of these excitations adheres to the values predicted by composite fermion theory.

This study introduces a novel finite element framework for solving Stokes variational inequalities encountered in glaciological contexts, specifically addressing the modeling of basal slip. The approach involves reformulating the problem as a mixed-type system comprising a Stokes equation and a complementarity condition. To resolve this system, the authors employ a projection technique combined with a penalty method. The work establishes the convergence of the proposed scheme and provides detailed numerical results from experiments that validate this convergence.

We have compiled a novel sample of 13 starbursting galaxies, each exhibiting a mass outflow flux exceeding $10\,M_\odot\,\text{yr}^{-1}\,\text{kpc}^{-2}$ and a star formation surface density surpassing $1\,M_\odot\,\text{yr}^{-1}\,\text{kpc}^{-2}$. These systems were identified through a thorough search of the literature for high-redshift ($z>0.5$) sources displaying both strong outflows and vigorous star formation. Our analysis reveals that the outflow mass fluxes in these objects are comparable to those in local starburst galaxies, implying that the physical mechanisms driving mass loss remain consistent across this vast redshift range. Furthermore, the outflow mass fluxes correlate with star formation surface density, a relationship that mirrors findings from local systems. We also observed that the outflow mass fluxes are roughly a factor of two lower than the mass inflow fluxes, a disparity that may stem from the fact that outflows are often only a partial response to star formation. Additionally, the outflow momentum fluxes align with those of local starbursts, suggesting that the momentum imparted to galactic outflows is largely independent of redshift.

The ALICE collaboration has recently released measurements of triangular flow ($v_3$) in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV, covering centralities from 0–5% to 5–20%. These findings are compared with $p$-Pb data to evaluate initial geometric effects on $v_3$ and to benchmark them against theoretical models. The study also examines the centrality dependence of $v_3$ in $p$-Pb collisions, specifically addressing the role of event-plane fluctuations in $p$-Pb interactions.

This paper introduces a transparent mechanism for synchronizing robot maneuvers within a robotic swarm, enabling the explicit modeling of inter-robot interactions. By utilizing a virtual spring connecting each robot to its leader, this approach facilitates a clear representation of the forces exerted by neighboring agents. The study presents a straightforward controller designed to achieve transparent force transmission, ensuring that the aggregate forces from the swarm are conveyed to the individual robots. Simulation results validate the efficacy of this controller, confirming its ability to enable precise transmission of forces from the group to each member.

We introduce a novel self-supervised approach for pre-training deep neural networks for semantic segmentation by leveraging depth estimation from unlabeled video data. Our method utilizes a framework that trains a segmenter using a combination of a standard classification loss and a novel depth-based pseudo-labeling strategy. This strategy generates reliable pseudo-labels by analyzing temporal inconsistencies in pixel intensities to produce per-pixel depth maps, which are then used to refine the initial depth estimates. We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset, demonstrating that pre-training with our proposed self-supervised approach yields significant performance gains over standard supervised pre-training methods.

Bohr's inequality asserts that for any power series $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n z^n$ with a unit disk convergence region, the inequality $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_n|r^n \leq \|f\|_{\infty}$ must hold, where $\|f\|_{\infty}$ represents the supremum norm. This paper introduces a novel refinement of Bohr's radius defined as $R_{\text{new}}(f) = \max\{r \in [0,1) : \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_n|r^n \leq \|f\|_{\infty}\}$. We demonstrate that this new parameter provides a sharper bound compared to the traditional radius and provide several applications of this result.

Kendall's tau serves as a widely recognized nonparametric metric for correlation. This paper introduces a novel estimator for Kendall's tau that is specifically designed for high-dimensional datasets, where the number of variables is comparable to or exceeds the sample size. The proposed approach utilizes a graph-based framework to derive a consistent estimator, even in such high-dimensional scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic normality of this estimator when the sample size surpasses the dimensionality. To address cases where the sample size is not larger than the number of variables, we develop a bootstrap methodology to derive critical values. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our estimator outperforms existing alternatives in terms of statistical efficiency.

The integration of Internet of Things (IoT) and Edge Computing has significantly advanced the capabilities of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). By deploying Edge Intelligence Systems (EIS) at the network edge, ITS can leverage local data to deliver real-time services, thereby reducing latency and alleviating bandwidth constraints. However, the limited storage and computational resources inherent to edge devices pose significant challenges for executing complex, data-intensive ITS applications. To address this, this paper introduces a novel framework known as Federated Edge Intelligence (FEI). FEI combines the advantages of EIS with federated learning (FL), enabling collaborative training of a global model across multiple edge devices without transferring sensitive local data. This approach ensures data privacy while optimizing the use of constrained edge resources. Furthermore, the study evaluates the performance of FEI within a simulated ITS environment, specifically analyzing the impact of FL hyperparameters on model convergence and the trade-off between communication overhead and training efficiency.

The Euler characteristic is a fundamental topological invariant widely utilized in algebraic topology, differential topology, and global analysis. In this paper, we present a novel algorithm for computing it within metric measure spaces, specifically targeting spaces that admit an almost splitting at infinity. Building on this contribution, we also introduce a new regularity criterion for metric measure spaces, establishing conditions under which the Euler characteristic is well-defined.

This study examines a predator-prey model incorporating a strong Allee effect, where the predator relies on a specific functional response to locate prey. It is demonstrated that the system possesses a unique co-existence equilibrium point, which is globally stable within a specific region of the phase space. Conversely, the system exhibits three boundary equilibrium points, two of which are stable while the third is unstable. Numerical simulations illustrate that the long-term fate of both populations is contingent upon their initial conditions. Specifically, the predator population either persists or becomes extinct depending on whether the initial state lies within the basin of attraction corresponding to the stable equilibrium points or those leading to extinction.

The Hirsch conjecture, proposed in 1967, hypothesized that any $d$-dimensional polytope with $n$ facets has a diameter no more than $n-d$. Although this conjecture was disproven in 2000 by Kahl and Santos, the underlying question remains a significant topic in discrete geometry. This paper introduces a novel approach to the diameter problem by leveraging a specific class of polytopes defined through a combinatorial framework. We demonstrate that for these polytopes, the diameter is bounded above by a function of $n$ that is sublinear with respect to dimension, thereby supporting the original intuition behind the Hirsch conjecture.

In this work, we demonstrate that for any associative ring $R$ possessing $k$ torsion within its group of units, the corresponding nil-group $\mathrm{nil}_R$ also exhibits $k$ torsion. Additionally, we outline a method for determining the exponent of torsion elements within these nil-groups.

We have developed a novel computational framework designed to evaluate the off-shell and non-resonant contributions to the $e^+e^-\to\tau^+\tau^-\bar{\nu}_\tau\nu_\tau$ process, specifically focusing on the extraction of the charged tau neutrino mass. This method employs a Monte Carlo technique to handle the high-dimensional phase space, utilizing a specific parametrization of the five-body decay to isolate the tau neutrino mass effects. We demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of accurately quantifying these off-shell contributions, a feature essential for conducting precise tests of the Standard Model.

The widespread deployment of security-critical systems, such as facial recognition, has intensified concerns regarding privacy and the necessity for robust anti-spoofing and liveness detection. While deep learning has become the standard for detecting presentation attacks, current methods often rely on single-layer architectures that struggle to capture the complex, multi-layered nature of these attacks. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-layer deep learning framework designed to identify spoofing attacks. Our approach utilizes three distinct layers, each targeting specific attack characteristics: a shallow layer for texture analysis, a middle layer for color analysis, and a deep layer for structural analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that this multi-layer model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an Area Under the Curve (AUC) score of 0.9999 on the Deepfake Face Detection 2019 dataset.

The primary hurdle in applying supervised learning to autonomous driving is the scarcity of real-world data. While data augmentation is a common strategy to synthesize training samples from limited real data, it often fails to account for the temporal correlations inherent in driving sequences. This study introduces a novel framework for data augmentation that leverages recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to generate synthetic sequences. The approach utilizes a teacher network trained on genuine driving data to instruct a student network that creates synthetic data based on a small set of real sequences. The synthesized data is then incorporated into the teacher's training regimen, effectively enhancing the student's ability to predict future driving states. The efficacy of this method is validated across three key tasks: end-to-end autonomous driving, trajectory prediction, and lane-keeping assistance.

Parallel evolutionary algorithms (PEAs) are frequently employed to accelerate search processes, yet they often yield performance that is unpredictable and inconsistent. A primary source of this variability is the asynchronous nature of PEAs, which allows individuals to be evaluated at varying times. This timing disparity introduces an evaluation time bias, where individuals evaluated at shorter durations receive fewer mutations and thus have a reduced probability of being selected. This study investigates the impact of evaluation time bias on the efficacy of such algorithms by analyzing the behavior of a simple $(1+1)$ parallel evolutionary algorithm. The findings indicate that this timing disparity can lead to a significant decline in search performance, a conclusion supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical simulations. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the magnitude of this degradation is contingent upon the degree of parallelism utilized.

We examine the system's origin using a statistical framework that accounts for the planet-host mass-ratio distribution, the semi-major axis distribution, and the host star mass distribution. Our analysis indicates that the planet-host mass-ratio distribution is the primary factor in this system's existence. This study investigates the effective time-independent Floquet generator within a periodically driven open quantum system, revealing that the system's evolution is governed by the effective Hamiltonian and an effective dissipative map. The research identifies two distinct phases: a paramagnetic phase, where the effective dynamics resemble those of the static time-averaged counterpart, and a Floquet many-body localized (FMBL) phase, characterized by strong effective dissipation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the steady state in the FMBL phase is determined by the eigenstates of the effective Hamiltonian, which is a defining characteristic of this regime.

We investigated the magnetic and transport characteristics of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ across the full rhodium concentration range ($0 \le x \le 1$). For mixtures exceeding $x \approx 0.6$, CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ displays antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering, whereas lower concentrations exhibit Kondo lattice behavior. This AFM state is attributed to the presence of Rh moments, which couple antiferromagnetically with Ce moments. Notably, the AFM transition temperature ($T_N$) peaks at $x = 0.8$ ($T_N = 17.5$ K), a value significantly higher than that observed in pure Rh (where $T_N = 26.7$ K).

We report the detection of HI narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) in the high-mass star-forming region W51 Main using the 21-cm line. This study is the first to identify HINSA in a high-mass star-forming region (SFRC) outside the Milky Way. The observations were conducted with the Green Bank Telescope at a distance of 2.4 kpc, revealing a main emission peak at a velocity of 10.5 km/s with a width of 1.5 km/s. The self-absorption feature appears at 10.1 km/s with a width of 0.2 km/s. The region's kinematics are modeled as a combination of a main body and a foreground cloud, with the HINSA signal likely originating from the main body. The main body is estimated to have a mass of 10^4 solar masses and a radius of 0.5 pc. The study also explores the potential causes of HINSA in the main body, including the effects of stellar radiation pressure and the influence of a magnetic field. The results suggest that the magnetic field is the primary driver of the HINSA signal in the main body. This paper investigates the ergodic properties of intermediate beta-transformations, specifically maps of the form $T_{\alpha,p}(x) = \alpha x + p \pmod 1$ where $\alpha$ is a real parameter greater than 1 and $p$ is an integer parameter satisfying $1 \leq p \leq \alpha - 2$. We demonstrate that these maps are ergodic and possess no absolutely continuous invariant measures. Furthermore, we establish that for a parameter $\alpha$ within a Lebesgue measurable set of positive measure, the map $T_{\alpha,p}$ exhibits topological mixing. Our findings indicate a strong relationship between intermediate beta-transformations and greedy transformations with a hole at zero, specifically showing that $T_{\alpha,p}$ shares the same invariant Cantor set as the greedy map $T_{\text{greedy},0}$. Consequently, the dynamics of intermediate beta-transformations can be analyzed through their correspondence with greedy beta-transformations featuring a hole at zero.

This study reports on the measurement of the $\phi_s$ phase, associated with mixing-induced CP violation in $B_s^0$ decays, alongside the determination of the $B_s^0$ lifetime. The analysis utilizes 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb detector at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The results yield $\phi_s = -0.06 \pm 0.11$ (stat.) $^{+0.03}_{-0.04}$ (syst.) rad and $\tau_{B_s^0} = 0.469 \pm 0.007$ (stat.) $\pm$ 0.013 (syst.) ps.

Recent research has highlighted the difficulty deep networks face in generalizing to target datasets that differ from their training distributions. This challenge is particularly acute in medical imaging, where training data often originates from a single institution, creating a significant gap when deploying models across different hospitals. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that combines deep networks with a generative model capable of learning a shared latent space for multiple source datasets. This framework trains a new architecture that maps inputs from all sources into this unified latent space, enabling the network to generate images that appear as if they were created from the target domain. We validate our method using MRI images from the MNI template as the target and data from three distinct hospitals as sources. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully synthesizes realistic MNI images from the training hospitals, effectively bridging the distribution gap.

In the plane over $\mathbb{F}_q$, an arc is defined as a collection of $q+2$ points with no three being collinear. This study investigates arcs of length $q+2$ within the Desarguesian plane $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ that are not contained in any generalized conic. We demonstrate that any such arc is a generalized elliptic cone curve, a result that extends previous findings by Thas and Sz\H{o}nyi, who established this property only for lengths $q+4$ when $q$ is odd.

This paper presents a closed-form formula for the count of equilateral triangles in a regular triangular grid that has $n$ vertices on each side. Although regular triangles of varying orientations may appear in such grids, this work focuses exclusively on equilateral triangles.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved significant success in numerous domains, their opacity has hindered widespread adoption. Current leading interpretability methods for GNNs primarily focus on post-hoc explanations, which identify input features responsible for a specific prediction. However, these approaches fail to account for the substantial influence of learned node embeddings on those predictions. Consequently, explanations derived solely from input features may be inaccurate or misleading. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework for generating faithful explanations of GNN predictions. Our approach employs a counterfactual method that integrates both input features and node embeddings, thereby offering a more accurate characterization of the factors driving predictions. Empirical evaluations on various graph classification and node classification benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior faithfulness compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We report the discovery of RXCJ0232.2-4420, a galaxy cluster identified through X-ray observations by the eROSITA telescope. Located at a redshift of $z=0.292$, it is the most distant cluster confirmed by X-ray observations to date. Analysis of its X-ray spectrum reveals a cool core, characterized by a central temperature of $0.7$ keV and a central entropy of $100$ erg cm$^{-2}$. Additionally, the cluster exhibits a steep entropy gradient and a significant entropy deficit, indicating that it has never undergone a major merger. We estimate its mass to be $M_{500} = (1.1 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$ and its redshifted temperature to be $kT_{500} = 7.0$ keV. These findings suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a massive, massive cluster that has not yet reached virial equilibrium. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of galaxy clusters at high redshift.

This paper introduces a novel recurrent memory architecture called the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), which integrates classical control theory with deep learning. By utilizing control-theoretic principles, the LMU enables recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to manage long-term dependencies, effectively addressing the limitations inherent in standard RNNs, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, and transformers. Specifically, the LMU employs discrete orthogonal Legendre polynomials to generate a sequence of hidden states that capture the continuous trajectory of a system. This approach allows for the precise approximation of continuous dynamics, thereby enhancing the RNN's ability to model long-term behaviors. Empirical evaluations across various tasks demonstrate that the LMU outperforms established baselines, including LSTMs and transformers, in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

The discovery of new physics at the LHC could profoundly reshape our understanding of fundamental matter, dark matter, and the universe's evolution. Feblly interacting particles (FIPs) are a compelling candidate for dark matter, offering testable predictions for the LHC. This review examines the status of FIP research, highlighting both theoretical frameworks and experimental strategies. We explore the distinctive signatures of LHC searches for FIPs and outline the challenges inherent in identifying them.

We investigate the co-evolution of language and mobility within a population of $N$ individuals, where each person possesses a linguistic trait and a migration trait. The language trait is binary, representing one of two languages, while the migration trait is continuous, determining an individual's propensity to move to a neighboring site with a certain probability. Language evolution follows a replicator dynamic, where individuals adopt the language of their neighbors, whereas migration traits evolve via natural selection, favoring those who migrate more frequently if they achieve higher reproductive success. We demonstrate that migration drives the spontaneous emergence of monolingual islands—regions where individuals share the same language—which in turn create selective pressures for increased migration traits among island members. This positive feedback loop results in a stable polymorphism, maintaining both language and migration diversity within the overall population.

This study examines the convergence of neural networks (NNs) trained on periodic solutions to generic linear PDEs characterized by high-frequency components. We establish that for NNs with fixed width, training via gradient descent on standard loss functions yields convergence rates that are suboptimal with respect to network complexity. Conversely, we demonstrate that NNs with sufficient width can achieve optimal convergence. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings through experiments on a periodic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation.

This study examines the optimal energy decay rates for a coupled wave system incorporating Kelvin-Voigt damping and Kozlov-Neumann-Kelley (KNC) boundary conditions. While previous research established polynomial decay with a rate of $t^{-1/4}$ for interior damping, this work demonstrates a significantly faster decay of $e^{-c t^{1/4}}$ when damping is applied partially, even under the constraints of KNC conditions. This improvement aligns with findings regarding optimal dissipation observed in other contexts involving similar boundary setups.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has become a powerful tool for tackling complex decision-making tasks, yet it suffers from high computational costs and a tendency to overfit. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a new algorithm called the Multi-Task Ensemble Policy Gradient (MTEPG). This method employs a policy network designed to simultaneously optimize for multiple tasks within a single framework. By leveraging task correlations, the MTEPG approach enhances sample efficiency, reduces the risk of overfitting, and generates more robust policies. We evaluated the algorithm on both single-task and multi-task benchmarks, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of sample efficiency and final performance.

Nonreciprocity, typically achieved via optical isolators and circulators that rely on bulky magneto-optical components, is often incompatible with the tight integration requirements of modern photonic systems. This paper introduces a novel optical nonreciprocity mechanism based on optical parametric squeezing within a cavity. By modulating the intracavity intensity at a frequency equal to twice the detuning between the pump laser and the cavity resonance, we generate squeezed light. This squeezing induces a direction-dependent shift in the cavity resonance frequency, thereby creating nonreciprocity. The proposed method is experimentally validated using a micropillar cavity integrated with a periodically poled lithium niobium waveguide, demonstrating a tunable optical nonreciprocity bandwidth of 10 MHz.

This study examines the optimization of deep networks with a single hidden layer, specifically analyzing the relationship between the number of local maxima and the network's width. We demonstrate that for models utilizing concave kernel functions, the count of local maxima remains bounded independently of width, a property that supports the hypothesis that such functions facilitate easier optimization. Furthermore, we establish that these functions can approximate standard sigmoidal mappings while maintaining superior generalization capabilities.

CRESST operates as a direct dark matter detection initiative utilizing calcium-aluminum silicate crystals cooled to millikelvin temperatures. This setup enables the simultaneous tracking of both phonon and temperature variations within the crystals, facilitating the identification of light particles with masses as low as 0.1 GeV. This paper introduces a new analysis method for CRESST data that employs a Bayesian framework to determine the likelihood of light particle interactions. This approach utilizes a Bayesian hierarchical model featuring a flexible functional form for the differential cross-section, which is defined by a set of basis functions. The resulting posterior distribution for these basis function coefficients is derived using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. By applying this technique to CRESST data, we establish stringent constraints on light dark matter interactions, specifically targeting WIMP-nucleon cross-sections and the branching ratio for dark matter annihilation into di-electron pairs.

This study introduces a novel approach to image deblurring that leverages a learned kernel mixture model. By employing a kernel mixture structure, the method effectively captures diverse blur characteristics inherent in real-world scenes. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is utilized to synthesize image pairs consisting of a clean original and its corresponding blurred version generated by the learned kernel mixtures. The proposed framework is then trained on these synthetic pairs to develop a deblurring network capable of reversing the blur. Experimental results indicate that this approach surpasses existing methods in both performance and efficiency.

This paper introduces the associative commutative Hom-Yang-Baxter pair and its corresponding invariant associative commutative Hom-Yang-Baxter pair, demonstrating that the latter generates the double non-abelian variant of the variant curved Hom-Yang-Baxter system.

Formal methods are commonly employed to mathematically verify software correctness, with Hoare logic serving as a foundational approach for reasoning about program behavior. However, manually constructing these formal proofs is often labor-intensive and difficult to master. This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically generating Hoare logic proofs by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs). We propose a prompt engineering strategy that utilizes GPT-3.5 Turbo to synthesize missing preconditions and postconditions for specific program statements. Our method is evaluated across three distinct scenarios: verifying correctness assertions for given programs, identifying statements within a program that violate specific assertions, and inferring missing assertions for a provided program. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves an average accuracy of 70.4% in scenario 1, 71.2% in scenario 2, and 72.4% in scenario 3.

Distributed consensus protocols, including those found in blockchains and distributed databases, are essential for coordinating tasks across multiple machines. This paper introduces Canopus, a novel consensus protocol designed to efficiently manage such coordination. Canopus achieves this by leveraging a distributed shortest path algorithm to distribute the voting process, thereby reducing the number of messages exchanged. The protocol's performance is evaluated through extensive simulations, which demonstrate that Canopus surpasses existing solutions in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness.

We have conducted extensive molecular dynamics simulations of a mixed lipid bilayer composed of POPC and cholesterol, varying the cholesterol concentration from 0% to 40%. The study analyzes how this variation affects the bending modulus, excess free energy of mixing, and the distribution of bilayer thickness. The results indicate that cholesterol's inclusion stiffens the bilayer, with the bending modulus rising linearly up to 20% content before plateauing. Additionally, the free energy of mixing remains nearly constant regardless of cholesterol concentration, while the bilayer thickness distribution shifts to a thinner profile in the presence of cholesterol.

This study examines the evolution of anisotropic loop quantum cosmology models featuring a massless scalar field, specifically focusing on anisotropy dynamics, the critical threshold for quantum gravity effects, and the influence of these phenomena on cosmic evolution. We demonstrate that the critical matter density, which marks the onset of quantum gravity effects, is anisotropy-dependent, a finding that aligns with anisotropic predictions from loop quantum gravity. Our analysis reveals that the impact of anisotropy on the dynamics of the scale factor is negligible, allowing us to compare our results with those derived from isotropic loop quantum cosmology models. Consequently, we find that the critical density threshold in our anisotropic framework is lower than that observed in isotropic models.

The deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in robotics is growing, yet a significant hurdle remains: the lack of uncertainty quantification in their predictions. Without this, fully integrating DNNs into robotic systems is difficult. This paper introduces a novel uncertainty estimation method that utilizes a single, fully connected DNN. This approach is designed to be computationally efficient and compatible with various existing DNN architectures. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments on two real-world robotic tasks involving object detection and pose estimation.

Recent research has increasingly focused on enhancing the robustness of traffic predictions against data anomalies. While prior studies have largely examined this through the lens of temporal analysis, this work addresses spatial dimensions. We propose a novel approach that partitions test data into small, spatially cropped patches to facilitate prediction. Our hypothesis is that this method enhances robustness by enabling the model to focus on local spatial patterns, thereby reducing susceptibility to isolated noisy data points. Experimental results indicate that this patch-based framework is particularly effective for identifying and mitigating the impact of outliers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing state-of-the-art prediction models with minimal architectural changes.

We demonstrate that Gray categories serve as an alternative formulation of tricategories, wherein 2-functors mapping into Gray categories correspond precisely to opfibrations over correspondents. This insight enables a fresh perspective on constructing tricategories via correspondents, illustrated by deriving the category of fractions for a 2-category equipped with conflatable equivalences and formulating the quotient of a tricategory by an equivalence relation.

Accurately segmenting the hippocampus is crucial for diagnosing neuropsychiatric disorders, yet existing deep learning methods often fail to capture the organ's intricate internal structure. This study introduces a novel multi-level segmentation framework that leverages the unique morphology of the hippocampus. The proposed architecture integrates a multi-level decoder with a specialized decoder tailored to the hippocampus, which utilizes a novel internal structure loss function. This function is designed to enhance the model's ability to grasp fine-grained details and internal organization. Additionally, a new hippocampus-specific dataset was created to support this research. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and performance metrics.

This work investigates a proposed three-particle extension of single-particle quantum interference, wherein three entities simultaneously traverse a two-path interferometer without any pair sharing a path. This scenario, known as "delocalized collision," is a suggested manifestation of higher-order quantum interference. We demonstrate that this setup can be realized using three-photon entangled states combined with standard beam splitters. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying beam splitter transmittances on the resulting state and outline potential experimental verification methods.

However, recent research indicates that this mechanism alone cannot account for the observed fluxes of high-energy protons. This study introduces a new acceleration mechanism that complements radial diffusion, specifically focusing on the acceleration of protons trapped in the outer belt through interactions with the Earth's magnetic field. The expressivity of deep neural networks (DNNs) is a critical determinant of their performance boundaries. Although numerous studies have examined theoretical expressivity, this work investigates the relationship between measured expressivity and actual DNN performance. We introduce a novel metric termed "learned complexity" to gauge the learnability of specific functions within a given DNN architecture. Our findings reveal a strong positive correlation between this learned complexity and performance outcomes across various tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that optimizing DNNs to minimize learned complexity can enhance their performance, a strategy that proves especially beneficial for shallow networks.

This study addresses low-rank matrix completion within a private setting, aiming to estimate a matrix $M^*$ using only partial observations while safeguarding sensitive user data. We introduce a novel algorithm that privately reconstructs the matrix by leveraging a privacy-preserving estimator of the Huber loss, which is robust against outliers. We establish that our method achieves optimal minimax lower bounds for both robustness and differential privacy, with these guarantees holding even when the matrix contains a sparse corruption. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach remains minimax optimal in the absence of any adversarial corruptions.

We introduce a novel technique for determining the size of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) by leveraging their observed vibrational spectra. This method relies on a comprehensive database of simulated spectra, which are generated using density functional theory (DFT) for various PAH structures. By comparing simulated and observed spectra, we identify the most probable molecular isomers corresponding to a given PAH. Furthermore, we employ a statistical analysis of these isomers to derive the average size of the molecules. When applied to interstellar dust, this approach yields a PAH size of approximately 1.2 nm, a figure that aligns well with previous estimates.

The detection of planets orbiting very low-mass stars is crucial for understanding planet formation theories. This study reports the discovery of a planet around the M6.5V star GJ 436B, utilizing 10 years of radial velocity data from the CORALIE spectrograph. Analysis of the data reveals a significant periodic signal with a period of 41.1 days and a semi-amplitude of 1.95 m/s. This signal is robust, with a false alarm probability of less than 0.1%, and is confirmed by a linear fit yielding a period of 41.0 days and a semi-amplitude of 1.93 m/s. Accounting for the star's rotation, the planet's orbital inclination, and its eccentricity, the study derives a minimum mass of 1.90 ± 0.14 M⊕. Additionally, the planet's semi-major axis is calculated to be 0.062 ± 0.002 AU, corresponding to an equilibrium temperature of 290 ± 10 K. This detection establishes that very low-mass stars can host planets with masses comparable to or smaller than Earth.

This study examines a graph-based puzzle where vertices represent lights, initially set to either on or off. Selecting a vertex toggles its own state and those of its neighbors. The objective is to reach a configuration where all lights are off. A graph is termed solvable if there exists an initial setup from which this goal state is reachable. We analyze the solvability of the hypercube $Q_n$ and the Moore graph $M_3$ under two scenarios: when $n$ is even and when $n$ is odd.

We introduce a novel approach to image segmentation that integrates a recently developed image restoration architecture. By leveraging the strengths of both image segmentation and image restoration models, our method effectively addresses the challenges of small training datasets and the difficulty of labeling large ones. The core of this approach involves a multi-scale image restoration framework that incorporates a new image segmentation model. This restoration framework utilizes a hierarchical structure with multiple pathways to capture both local and global image features. The image segmentation model is trained to output class probabilities for each pixel in an image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the challenging task of medical image segmentation, where we achieve state-of-the-art results on the MICCAI 2018 dataset.

Abstract interpretation is a static analysis method that approximates program behavior using iterative computations in a lattice structure, typically proceeding in ascending and descending phases to reach a fixed point. While the ascending phase is well-understood, the descending phase has received less attention. This paper introduces a new framework for abstract fixpoint computation that explicitly separates these phases into a widening step followed by a narrowing step. By isolating these processes, the approach allows for greater flexibility in selecting widening strategies and facilitates a more precise analysis of termination and complexity. Furthermore, the framework supports the use of multiple wideners and enablers within a single computation. The authors demonstrate the applicability of this method by reformulating established techniques—including standard widening, progressive computation, and computable post-fixpoints—within its structure.

Distance-based outlier detection is a prevalent unsupervised approach that does not rely on specific data distribution assumptions, offering broad applicability. However, its performance often suffers from the curse of dimensionality, particularly in high-dimensional contexts. To address this, we introduce a novel method that leverages the inherent low-dimensional manifold structure of high-dimensional data. By utilizing distances within these manifold structures, the proposed technique enhances outlier detection performance in high-dimensional settings. Empirical evaluations on both real-world and synthetic datasets confirm that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the spontaneous emission of a $^{87}$Rb($D_2$) atom situated near a conducting plane, with the plane's distance from the atom's center of mass varying between 10 and 100 $\mu$m. Theoretical predictions for the plane-induced modifications to the atom's spontaneous emission rate are compared against experimental measurements obtained using an optical pumping and repumping technique. The study finds that the experimental data aligns well with the theoretical model.

This study introduces a novel framework for achieving neighborhood fairness within graph neural networks (GNNs). Unlike existing graph-based fairness research that primarily focuses on node-level or edge-level metrics, our work targets the GNN neighborhood, a critical unit of analysis given that NLP and other tasks often depend on local graph structures. To address this, we propose a new metric termed the "neighborhood Gini coefficient," which quantifies inequality in node labels within a specific community. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm designed to minimize this metric by reassigning node labels to ensure fairer neighborhoods. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various real-world datasets, demonstrating that our method successfully enhances neighborhood fairness without compromising predictive accuracy.

This study introduces two methods for obtaining analytic approximate solutions to non-linear reaction equations, specifically the Michaelis-Menten equation and a reversible catalytic reaction model, utilizing the Homotopy Transform Method (HTM) and the Power Series Method (PSM). Both approaches yield results that closely align with numerical solutions generated via the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. Additionally, graphical representations illustrate the impact of varying parameters on the concentration of the product over time.

This study examines the squark pair production process at the LHC, where the squark subsequently decays into a gluino and a bottom quark. The resulting analysis focuses on the subsequent decay of the gluon into two jets, utilizing a data-driven technique to determine the gluon mass. The study demonstrates that this approach can probe a gluon mass range up to approximately 1.5 TeV, contingent on the virtual squark mass. Furthermore, the study investigates the sensitivity of the method to the gluon width, revealing that the derived gluon mass is robust against variations in the gluon width up to a value of 100 GeV.

This study examines the dynamics of financial bubbles within markets populated by heterogeneous arbitrageurs, who trade based on a common asset price while facing transaction costs. The model incorporates diverse agents characterized by distinct risk aversion levels, investment horizons, and endowments. We demonstrate that even when the fundamental value remains constant, bubbles can emerge and persist. Specifically, we identify that the coexistence of short-term arbitrageurs and long-term investors generates market conditions conducive to bubble formation. Furthermore, we establish that bubbles are sustained by a specific distribution of agents' horizons and risk preferences, which dictates the magnitude of the premium. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the size of these bubbles is contingent upon the proportion of long-term investors in the market.

This paper investigates the quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to constant forces and time-dependent linear couplings. We explicitly construct a complete set of eigenstates for this system and determine their complete temporal evolution. Additionally, we analyze the potential well's characteristics, focusing on energy spectra and state classification.

This study introduces a hybrid recommender system that integrates rating prediction with sentiment analysis. The proposed approach utilizes a neural network to forecast user ratings, incorporating as input the sentiment scores derived from textual reviews. To achieve this, we developed a Sentiment Analyzer to process text data and convert it into usable sentiment scores. These values are then merged with the user's historical rating data to form a composite feature vector, which serves as an input for the rating prediction model. The prediction engine itself is a neural network designed to estimate future ratings based on these enriched feature vectors. To validate the system's efficacy, we conducted experiments using the Amazon dataset, evaluating performance through Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). The results indicate that the proposed hybrid model outperforms traditional baseline methods in terms of both MSE and RMSE metrics.

Code-switching, defined as the seamless integration of multiple languages within a single utterance, is a prevalent phenomenon in human communication. However, current Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems are largely designed for single-language environments and struggle to handle such mixed content effectively. This paper introduces a novel approach to model code-switching by introducing a multilingual architecture that utilizes a shared embedding space for different languages, coupled with a dynamic language identification (LangID) mechanism. This component determines the specific language of each token and adjusts the model's processing strategy accordingly. The proposed framework is evaluated across three code-switching corpora to benchmark performance against existing methods. Results indicate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art systems in three distinct code-switching scenarios, specifically excelling in tasks involving tokenization, LangID detection, and part-of-speech tagging.

We demonstrate that any subgroup of a group of homeomorphisms on a compact surface which is bounded by the identity on each boundary component exhibits a specific structure: it contains a subgroup of rank three that ensures the entire group is not Roelcke precompact within its completion under the topology of pointwise convergence.

We examine integrable boundary conditions within the context of integrable deformations, specifically the $\lambda$-deformation, generalized Poisson-Lie $\rho$-deformation, and $q$-deformation. Our analysis highlights a strong relationship between these integrable boundary conditions and conformal brane geometries, with a particular focus on branes defined by conformal group actions. We also identify specific instances of $q$-deformation where the resulting $q$-branes are isomorphic to known solutions in the $\mathbb{C}P^3$ Wess-Zumino-Witten model.

Hexahedral mesh elements are widely regarded as the optimal choice for numerical computations in meshes. This study introduces a new, straightforward method for automatically generating such meshes, which relies on a combination of graph theory and a simple geometric algorithm. The process begins by creating a graph where nodes represent the corners of volume elements and edges represent their connections. Subsequently, a graph-based algorithm determines the necessary internal nodes and connections to define a structured grid. Finally, a geometric algorithm utilizes these graph-derived elements to construct the actual volume elements. The method's simplicity allows for the easy implementation of various features, such as the accommodation of curved boundaries and the handling of general boundary conditions.

Relation extraction (RE) is a natural language processing task focused on identifying relationships between entities within a text. While existing RE methods have largely relied on pre-trained language models, they often fail to leverage the abundant, unlabelled data available. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that integrates a pre-trained language model with a graph-based architecture to effectively capture relational information. Specifically, we leverage the pre-trained model to generate contextualized embeddings for words and phrases, which are then utilized to construct a relational graph. These graph-based representations are subsequently fed into an RE model to predict the specific relationships. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques on both single-task and multi-task RE datasets.

This paper introduces a compact, accurate, and precise compact model for deep submicron CMOS inverters. The model's parameters are derived through a rigorous analytical examination of inverter delay behavior, incorporating effects from parasitic capacitance, channel length modulation, velocity saturation, and drain-induced barrier lowering. These parameters are calculated using a straightforward closed-form equation. Validation against SPICE simulations confirms the model's high accuracy and simplicity.

This study introduces a novel approach to Lipschitz continuity Q-learning, a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that ensures convergence to an optimal Q-function within Lipschitz-continuous MDPs. By leveraging this property, our method constructs data-efficient policy evaluation steps that achieve sample-optimal statistical efficiency while maintaining the benefits of model-free learning. We further demonstrate that this approach is robust to estimation bias, a characteristic shared by many existing techniques.

Recent research indicates that animacy is processed as a continuum within the human ventral temporal cortex, with neural responses to stimuli varying systematically based on their degree of animacy. This study examined the extent to which two primary theories account for this phenomenon: the "animate object hypothesis," which posits a dedicated neural system for animate entities, and the "social complexity hypothesis," which suggests a continuum reflecting increasing social complexity. Utilizing data from a large-scale neural network model trained on diverse stimuli, we assessed the ability of both hypotheses to explain observed cortical responses. Our findings indicate that while both theories offer partial explanations, the social complexity hypothesis provides a superior account of the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex compared to the animate object hypothesis.

In scientific simulations, researchers frequently employ various methods to approximate key characteristics of a problem, such as concentration profiles, temperature distributions, or fluid flow patterns. This paper introduces a new approach to uncertainty quantification (UQ) that utilizes a Bayesian framework to assess the reliability of these approximations. The methodology is grounded in a probabilistic model of the underlying physical system, which is informed by available data and existing scientific knowledge. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a case study involving the modeling of heat transfer in a cylinder, showcasing its practical application.

Type-C QPOs are a newly identified class of X-ray variability observed in black hole X-ray transients, typically appearing during the hard and intermediate states of black hole transients. This study reports the detection of Type-C QPOs in the black hole binary candidate MAXI J1820+070, utilizing data from the Swift and NuSTAR satellites. We identified a Type-C QPO with a frequency of 0.11 Hz in the X-ray light curve recorded by Swift's XRT instrument during the source's hard state phase. Additionally, a Type-C QPO at 0.11 Hz was detected in the light curve obtained by NuSTAR's imaging calorimeter during the intermediate state. These findings suggest that the transition between hard and intermediate states in MAXI J1820+070 is accompanied by a shift in the accretion flow's geometry.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is frequently applied to cooperative scenarios, yet agents often struggle to generalize to unseen team members, resulting in brittle performance. This brittleness stems from agents learning to rely on specific partners' actions, creating a dependency that fails when those partners deviate. While prior research has addressed this in single-agent contexts, the problem remains largely unexplored in multi-agent environments. This paper introduces a solution to mitigate such dependencies through a multi-agent extension of the intrinsic variational autoencoder (IAVE). By utilizing intrinsic rewards derived from the IAVE, agents are guided to learn policies that are less contingent on specific teammates' actions. Empirical results across three cooperative tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces brittleness compared to standard baselines.

Identifying materials from visual input is a fundamental task with diverse applications, including industrial quality assurance, medical diagnostics, and robotics. Although recent advancements in material recognition have largely depended on massive datasets, this paper introduces a novel approach to tackle the challenge of recognizing materials from a single image without relying on large-scale training sets. We propose a new method that leverages a pre-trained general-purpose object detector to identify materials in unseen images. We introduce a new dataset, MAT10K, which contains 10,000 images of materials annotated with material classes. We further present a new method, SingleShot, which uses a pre-trained object detector to identify materials in unseen images. We investigate Lie 2-algebras arising from Manis 2-algebras, 2-algebras with a symmetric invariant inner product, and 2-algebras with symmetric invariant Riemannian metrics. We present examples of non-isomorphic Lie 2-algebras derived from Heisenberg and metaplectic groups, as well as the 2-groups associated with $SO(3)$, $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, and $SL(n,\mathbb{R})$. Furthermore, we examine Lie 2-cohomology for 2-algebras possessing a symmetric invariant inner product and the corresponding Chevalley-Eilenberg complex. Finally, we explore the Lie 2-algebra cohomology of the symmetric Lie 2-algebra linked to the symmetric Lie group $SO(n,\mathbb{R})$.

This study introduces a novel approach to local image feature matching that leverages the Transformer architecture. We hypothesize that the self-attention mechanism within Transformers can effectively capture long-range dependencies in image patches, thereby enhancing the robustness of descriptors in regions lacking distinct textures. To address the high computational cost typically associated with Transformers, we suggest a lightweight variant utilizing a limited receptive field. Experiments conducted on the OpenMMLab "RANSAC-Lift-Synth" benchmark demonstrate that our method, named "Light-TR," surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both descriptor and matching performance. Furthermore, our implementation achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to standard Transformer-based models.

We investigate the polarization properties of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line-of-sight ($B_\perp$) in the solar photosphere, utilizing data from the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Our analysis focuses on the first-order moments of the relative linear polarization degree ($Q/I$) and circular polarization degree ($U/I$) within the $B_\perp$ line-of-sight of sight (LOS) component. We examine these measurements across various spatial scales and under different atmospheric conditions. Our findings indicate that the observed bias in $B_\perp$ is primarily driven by the non-uniform distribution of the LOS parallel component ($B_\parallel$) rather than by the inclination angle distribution itself. Furthermore, we observe that the magnitude of this bias is significantly affected by the optical depth of the layer being probed.

This paper introduces a novel pricing mechanism designed to motivate consumers to shift their peak-time energy usage to off-peak periods, thereby reducing the load on the power grid. The proposed scheme utilizes a distributed approach where consumers autonomously determine their energy consumption schedules based on specific cost functions. The utility provider establishes a power distribution network that incorporates a distributed control algorithm for managing power distribution. The paper provides a formal analysis of the system's convergence and demonstrates its performance through extensive simulations.

This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of charged black strings situated in asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetime, employing the extended thermodynamic framework. By applying the canonical ensemble, we identify a first-order Hawking-Page phase transition. Furthermore, within the grand canonical ensemble, we demonstrate that charged strings can undergo a second-order phase transition, which aligns with the findings regarding the black hole transition.

This paper examines the power-law decay exponents found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for weighted $L^2$-functions, where these exponents are linked to the corresponding pointwise scaling exponents of a spectral measure. Specifically, we establish that for any $\alpha \in (0,+\infty)$, there exists a spectral measure $\sigma$ such that every function $f \in L^2(\sigma)$ yields a weakly almost periodic (w.a.p.) sequence $(T^n f)_{n\geq 0}$ characterized by the exponent $\alpha$. Additionally, we demonstrate that for any $\alpha \in (0,+\infty)$, there exists a spectral measure $\sigma$ such that the sequence $(T^n f)_{n\geq 0}$ converges to zero in weighted $L^2(\sigma)$ with the power-law exponent $\alpha$.

The study of metal-poor stars is essential for understanding the origins of the Galaxy, its chemical evolution, and early star formation. This research presents high-resolution spectroscopic data for 12 stars with [Fe/H] < -2.5, located in the Galactic bulge and disk, covering 13 elements ranging from Na to Y. These stars were selected to have a wide range of [Fe/H] values and [Fe/H] - [Fe/H] ratios. The derived abundances are compared with those of bulge and disk field stars, as well as those found in the Magellanic Clouds. The results indicate that bulge and disk stars share similar abundance patterns, but bulge stars exhibit higher [X/Fe] ratios for most elements. The study also compares these findings with data from the Magellanic Clouds, noting that bulge and disk stars resemble each other more closely than either does the Magellanic Clouds.
